questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: What we've learnt about Covid after a year
The history of the Spanish flu in 1918
How to wash your hands properly
Why flu is more dangerous than Covid
questions.why: Georgina says it's good to take stock a year on and see how our knowledge has changed.

questions.q: When did reports of a new flu-like infection first come from China?
options: In early 2021
In the summer of 2019
At the end of December 2019
questions.why: Neil says reports first came out of China at the end of December 2019.

questions.q: How did ordinary people help stop the virus spreading, according to Georgina?
options: By helping to make vaccines in local factories
By washing hands, wearing masks and staying home
By travelling much less to China and other countries
By sharing genetic information about the virus online
questions.why: She says we played our part by washing our hands, wearing masks and staying at home.

questions.q: Why did Jenny Rohn say the new virus looked 'wimpy' at first?
options: Because it only seemed to affect young and healthy people
Because scientists already had a vaccine ready to use
Because it didn't seem to spread between people at all
Because seasonal flu infects many more people every year
questions.why: She says flu makes the Wuhan virus look wimpy because of the sheer number of people it infects.

questions.q: What was Jenny Rohn worried about?
options: That if the virus spread like flu, many people would die
That seasonal flu would disappear from the world completely
That testing for the virus would be too expensive for most
That people would soon get tired and stop wearing masks
questions.why: She says if it spread like flu all over the world, 'you would see a lot of people dead'.

questions.q: What does Dr Peter Daszak say about China's early response?
options: It was very slow to react to the virus
It kept the information secret
It had no system for finding new illnesses
It acted quite quickly
questions.why: He says the system kicked in within a couple of months of the first case: 'that's quite quick'.

questions.q: According to Dr Daszak, what helped scientists develop tests and vaccines quickly?
options: Money from governments around the world
Studying the Spanish flu
Publishing the virus's genetic code
Testing animals in zoos
questions.why: He says getting the full genome and making it publicly available helped rapidly develop tests and vaccines.

questions.q: What do the presenters hope vaccines will do?
options: Replace the need for tests
Be our way out of the pandemic
Stop seasonal flu
Make masks unnecessary in hospitals
questions.why: Georgina says the vaccines are 'hopefully our way out of this pandemic'.
